LINSEIS Thermomechanical Analysis TMA
Product catalog summary
Introduction to Thermomechanical Analysis (TMA)
Thermomechanical Analysis (TMA) is a technique used to measure sample displacement such as growth, shrinkage, and movement as a function of temperature, time, and applied force. It is primarily used to characterize linear expansion, glass transitions, and softening points of materials by applying a constant force while varying temperature.
Typical Applications
Tension studies of films and fibers
Determination of softening behavior and glass transition temperatures
Phase change determination and mechanical behavior under force
Determination of expansion coefficient and sintering behavior
General Features
High resolution for measuring nanometer changes
Dynamic Load TMA for weak transitions and elasticity
Wide measuring range from -150°C to 1600°C
Gas tight cell for controlled measurement environment
Technical Specifications
The TMA system includes a sample chamber with controlled temperature and atmosphere, a robust furnace for rapid heating and cooling, and a precise expansion and temperature sensor. The Dynamic TMA mode allows for the study of visco-elastic behavior.
Software Features
PC controlled with Microsoft Windows compatibility
Includes modules for temperature control, data acquisition, and evaluation
Features such as data security, curve comparison, and statistical evaluation
TMA / DTMA Features
Linear thermal expansion evaluation
Phase transformation and sinter process evaluation
Visco-elastic behavior with dynamic load
Applications and Case Studies
Polyvinylchloride (PVC): Used as an electrical insulator, with a glass point detected at 93.2°C.
Silicon Rubber: Performs well in extreme temperatures, with a glass point at -54.9°C.
Elastomers: Used in various industries, with a glass point detected at 29.9°C.
Polycarbonate (PC): Softening occurs before the glass transition temperature is reached.
